# Exercises: Softmax Policies on a Two-Armed Bandit

These exercises accompany our notes on policy gradients. Each one asks you to work out by hand what a small softmax policy does on a two-armed bandit, so that the general update rule stops being a formula and becomes something you can predict before running any code. Solutions are at the end of the page; try each exercise before reading them.
Write down the policy. With one parameter per arm, the policy is \pi_\theta(a) = \frac{\exp(\theta_a)}{\sum_{b} \exp(\theta_b)}. Show that adding the same constant to both parameters leaves the policy unchanged, and explain why this means one of the two parameters can be fixed at zero without loss.
Compute the gradient of the log-probability. Show that \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a) = \mathbf{e}_a - \pi_\theta, where \mathbf{e}_a is the indicator vector of arm a. What is the expected value of this vector when a is drawn from the policy itself?
Expected update. Let the two arms pay \mu_1 and \mu_2 on average. Write the expected policy-gradient step \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_\theta}[r(a) \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a)] in terms of \mu_1, \mu_2 and the probability p of the first arm. For which value of p is the step largest?
A baseline. Subtracting a constant b from every reward does not change the expected step. Prove this, and then compute the variance of the single-sample step as a function of b. Show that the variance is smallest when b is close to the average reward, and say what happens to learning when b is chosen far too high.
Entropy bonus. Add \lambda H(\pi_\theta), with H(\pi) = -\sum_a \pi(a) \log \pi(a), to the objective. Find the fixed point of the expected update as a function of \lambda and the gap \Delta = \mu_1 - \mu_2, and sketch how the probability of the better arm at the fixed point changes as \lambda grows from zero.
Natural gradient. The information matrix of this policy is F(\theta) = \mathrm{diag}(\pi_\theta) - \pi_\theta \pi_\theta^\top. Show that it is singular, relate its null space to the first exercise, and compute the natural-gradient step using the pseudo-inverse.
Solutions
The policy only depends on differences of parameters, because the shared factor \exp(c) cancels between the numerator and the denominator. The expected log-probability gradient is zero, which is the identity behind the baseline exercise. The expected step is proportional to p(1-p)\Delta, which is largest at p = 1/2 and vanishes as the policy becomes deterministic.
